cells.tense: You are at the table this hour, and the joy is already rising.
cells.act: reconcile what you know with what you feel about it
cells.ask: Set what you know about these people beside what you feel toward them, and take the single move that fits both.
cells.core:
A shared moment is happening and the joy wants to be passed around like bread. What keeps it good is small handiwork: noticing who has gone quiet, letting someone else take the next toast, moving a chair. You do that part easily and well, and it rarely gets named.

To keep it honest, line up what you actually know about these people with what you feel toward them, and let one plain move fall out of the pairing. This isn't a plan for managing the evening. It's enough that the share doesn't go by habit to whoever is loudest or nearest. Then your hands know what to do, and the celebration runs without you carrying the whole of it.
cells.verb: Raising joy together and letting it be shared
cells.place: Where fair shares get measured and brought back level

cells.tense: You will be bracing for a tomorrow that cannot be written in yet.
cells.act: return to the work daily until it is profound
cells.ask: Choose one shared thing that matters to you and give it ten minutes a day, no plan beyond today's part.
cells.core:
A future is being rehearsed before it arrives. You can see the next gathering, the next year, how it ought to go, and you keep reaching ahead to set it right. The people at the table tonight get a rehearsal of you instead of you. The joy isn't gone — it's being spent on a night that hasn't happened.

What helps is not to care less. Put your hands on the real thing and stay with it a little, daily. Pick one shared thing you care about and do today's part of it, no more, and leave tomorrow's part for tomorrow. What actually needs to fall will fall once you stop holding the future up with your arms, and the room can have the person who is here.

cells.tense: You were standing at a threshold of a gathering you had already left.
cells.act: let the mind find its own limit in the thing
cells.ask: Take the question you quit early on — what you actually want from these people — and keep thinking till your mind runs out.
cells.core:
A gathering is going on and your coat is still on. The invitation came, the chair is yours, and you haven't quite arrived in it. That half-arriving isn't rudeness; it's a habit of keeping one foot back. Some ending in a shared room still has a hand on your sleeve, and tonight gets the version of you that is partly elsewhere.

You don't push yourself in. You stop at the edge and think. Take the question you have about these people — what you want from them, what you bring — and follow it further than you normally allow. Let it go until your mind hits its own limit, and remain there a moment rather than surfacing. The answer is allowed to be uncomfortable. That's where the real thing lives, and it walks you into the room without your having to perform arrival.

cells.tense: You are at the table, pen down, in a room you are already writing.
cells.act: sort the pieces into a shape you can act on
cells.ask: Before the next gathering, note what you want from it in a single line, then keep the paper closed until the evening's over.
cells.core:
Good feeling at a gathering has a keeper. Someone clocks who hasn't had a turn, whose laugh needs to land, whether the split came out even, and adjusts without a sound. Ask and the answer is that the group just works. It doesn't; it's being worked. Somebody is doing the evening's accounting, quietly, in the middle of it.

The change isn't to stop. It's to stand beside the doing. Before the next gathering, sort what you want from it into one line — not what the room needs, what you want — then fold it away and don't unfold it until the last plate is cleared. Later, reading it, you'll see the hand that wrote the line is the hand that kept the night level.
